blocks.html: Frequent experience will keep the reader from being astonished here: for daily we see many men and women slender, thin and delicate in their youth, who nevertheless, by the passage of time and the advancement of age, become stout, fat and cumbersome. And because the examples of this time might be odious to some, I shall have recourse to the most memorable of antiquity. Leo of Byzantium, the sophist, very lean in his first years, became so fat about his middle age that, being ambassador at Athens and mounted upon a high chair to appease some sedition, all the people, seeing him so excessively big and pot-bellied, began to laugh; whereupon Leo began to speak thus: WHAT IS IT that you laugh at, O Athenians, to see me so fat? Know that my wife is fatter still. And yet, when we are agreed, we two can well [lie] in a little bed; but on the contrary, when we are angry, the whole house is not enough for us. Which speech had so much grace and force with this people that it was forthwith appeased, and the sedition ceased. Dionysius of Heraclea, the tyrant, having been slender in his young years, became little by little so monstrously fat, paunchy and pot-bellied that he was constrained at night to apply a great quantity of leeches to his body, to suck out of him the excessive superfluity of the humour which made him so fat and corpulent. I leave aside Louis the Fat, thirty-ninth King of France, who flourished from the year 1110 to the year 1137, who became so immoderately big and fat that he carried away from it the surname of the Fat.
